description: I’m passionate about technology, programming, and solving real-world problems. I have experience with Arduino, web development, and building prototypes, including a posture-correcting device. I’m looking for creative, motivated teammates skilled in coding, data analysis, science, or design. I value teamwork, curiosity, and responsibility. Let’s combine our skills, use NASA’s open data, and build something meaningful together!
summary: Worst Sol is a layered, interactive Marswalk map that answers the question a crew cares about most: how far can we go and still get back when something fails? Users pick a base site among 13 real locations (nine NASA landing sites and four seen only from orbit), then stress-test it with four scenarios drawn from NASA mission history: a global dust storm (Opportunity, 2018), a solar flare (Curiosity, 2024), a reactor failure, and a missed landing. For each site the tool combines topography, atmospheric dust, temperature, radiation, and water data, plans the quickest walking route to real science targets around obstacles such as dunes, slopes, and cliffs, and returns a clear verdict: go, at your own risk, or no-go. It also maps the zone where a single failure is still survivable, simulates one sol of base power, and ranks sites by their weakest link instead of their average. The challenge asks for a layered view of a location or route that helps an astronaut plan a safe Marswalk and do new science. Worst Sol does this for the worst day, because that is the day that decides whether the crew comes home.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Worst Sol is a web tool for planning Marswalks around a future base. You choose a site on a map of Mars, then switch on stress tests and watch every number on the page react: the safe walking zone, the verdict for each science target, the base's power and the crew's day.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Site layer: coordinates, elevation, pressure, temperature range, daylight, sunlight per sol, and water and radiation for 13 sites, with the source named under each value.

2. Marswalk layer: a terrain map around the base (firm ground, rock, sand, slopes, and cliffs). A least-time pathfinding algorithm routes the walk around obstacles and computes time out, time on site, and time back against the suit's air supply.

3. Safety layer: the zone from which the crew can still reach shelter after one failure, by rescue rover or on foot. Dust storms slow travel, a reactor failure grounds the rover, and a solar flare leaves 45 minutes to reach shelter.

4. One sol at the base: sky, temperature, power generation, demand, and stored energy over a full sol, plus a 30-sol projection.

5. Crowd vs. algorithm: people vote for a site first, then see how it ranks when scored by its weakest link.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Crews and mission planners get a go, risk, or no-go answer for every target before the airlock opens. Students and the public get a 30-second vote-and-reveal that shows why Mars is dangerous. It runs in any browser, in English and Russian, with nothing to install.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Most maps plan for an average day. We plan for the worst one, and every scenario is anchored to a real event: Opportunity's solar energy falling from 645 to 22 watt-hours per sol in the 2018 storm and the record radiation dose Curiosity measured in May 2024.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in a single file; Canvas and SVG for maps and charts; NASA Mars Trek map tiles as the basemap; GitHub Pages for hosting.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED AND LIMITS

Astronaut safety comes first, so the tool reports the weakest link, not the average. Measured, computed, and estimated values are labeled separately in the app. The global basemap uses NASA Mars Trek mosaics; the terrain close to each base is a schematic built from mission reports, and values for the four sites without a landing are estimates. The next step is to replace the schematic terrain with HiRISE slope and THEMIS thermal-inertia layers.
